implementation_notes: The lock statement is the implicit lock: for an ordinary reference the compiler emits Monitor.Enter with try/finally Monitor.Exit, and when the argument is a System.Threading.Lock it emits a using over Lock.EnterScope(), whose ref-struct Dispose runs on every exit path - so release is a property of the block, not of the developer's memory. Other lock types (SemaphoreSlim, ReaderWriterLockSlim, async-lock libraries) follow the same shape when wrapped in an IDisposable guard and held by a using declaration (C# 8) or a using statement. Explicit Monitor.Enter/Exit or SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync with try/finally is justified only when the critical section must await, which a lock block cannot express.
pitfalls: You cannot await inside a lock block and Monitor is thread-affine, so an async critical section needs SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync plus a try/finally or a disposable release scope - not lock.
Locking on this, a Type or an interned string exposes the lock to unrelated code; use a dedicated private instance (ideally System.Threading.Lock).
A guard that is constructed but never assigned to a using variable is silently released nowhere: SemaphoreSlim.Wait() followed by an exception before Dispose leaks the permit.

variants.name: ambient transactions (TransactionScope / Transaction.Current)
variants.implementation_notes: The enterprise form of Implicit Lock on .NET: an ambient transaction - a TransactionScope, or Transaction.Current set by the container - makes connections, commands and other resource managers enlist automatically, so isolation and locking are decided by the resource managers rather than by the business method, and the scope's Complete() versus Dispose() decides commit or rollback. Use it when one operation spans several resources and the infrastructure must coordinate the locks; an explicit DbTransaction is still the simpler and justified choice for a single connection to a single resource, where scope promotion and distributed-transaction machinery are pure overhead.
pitfalls: Forgetting scope.Complete() rolls the work back silently, and connections stay enlisted until Dispose runs; an exception before Complete() is the intended rollback path, not a bug to swallow.

Awaiting inside a TransactionScope without TransactionScopeAsyncFlowOption.Enabled loses the ambient transaction on the continuation, and with connection pooling the second resource can silently promote the transaction to a distributed one.

Nested scopes join the ambient transaction by default (TransactionScopeOption.Required), so an inner step that must be independent needs Suppress or RequiresNew - otherwise its failure aborts the outer transaction.
